lessons.title: Oil and Gas, Power, and Utilities: Regulated Returns and Government Pricing

body.text: In most sectors, the market sets prices. In oil, gas, and power, the government and regulators often do. That single fact flips the usual analysis: a regulated utility can be indifferent to the price of coal, while a fuel retailer can lose money in a quarter when crude soars and pump prices stay frozen. Before you analyse these companies, find out who sets the price.

children.text: This part of the market holds some of India's largest companies: Reliance Industries, ONGC, Indian Oil, BPCL, HPCL, GAIL, NTPC, Power Grid, Tata Power, and the city gas distributors. Many are majority-owned by the government, pay high dividends, and trade at low multiples. Understanding them means understanding regulation as much as economics.
The Oil and Gas Value Chain: Three Very Different Businesses

markDefs.definition: Gross Refining Margin: the difference between the value of petroleum products a refinery produces and the cost of the crude oil it processes, usually quoted in US dollars per barrel.

children.text: For refiners, the number that matters is

. A refinery is essentially a conversion business: it buys crude, splits it into petrol, diesel, jet fuel, and other products, and earns the spread. Complex refineries that can process cheaper heavy and sour crude into high-value products usually earn higher margins than simple ones. Analysts compare a company's GRM with the Singapore benchmark margin, the reference price for Asian refiners.

body.latex: \text{GRM per barrel} = \text{Value of products per barrel} - \text{Cost of crude per barrel} \qquad \text{Annual gross margin} = \text{GRM} \times \text{Barrels processed per day} \times 365
body.caption: Refining margins are quoted per barrel, so throughput turns the spread into profit

body.title: Size the Refining Profit
body.prompt: A refinery processes 300,000 barrels of crude a day and earns a gross refining margin of $8 per barrel. Assuming it runs all 365 days, what is its annual gross refining margin, in $ million?
body.explanation: 300,000 barrels × $8 = $2.4 million a day. Over 365 days, that is $876 million. Now see the sensitivity: if GRM falls by just $2 a barrel, the annual figure drops to $657 million, a fall of $219 million with no change in volumes. Refining is a spread business, so margin per barrel matters more than the price of crude itself.

body.text: Fuel marketing is where government pricing shows up most starkly. When crude rises sharply and retail petrol, diesel, or LPG prices are held steady for policy reasons, oil marketing companies absorb the gap and can post losses in an otherwise strong year for the oil sector. When crude falls and pump prices stay put, the same companies earn unusually high marketing margins. Always separate refining margin from marketing margin.

body.title: Crude Spikes: Who Wins, Who Loses?
body.question: Brent crude jumps 30% in two months and the government asks fuel retailers to hold pump prices steady. Which company is most likely to benefit?
options: An integrated refining and fuel marketing company
A city gas distributor selling CNG to taxis
body.explanation: An upstream producer sells the crude it extracts, so it earns more when prices rise, subject to any government levy on windfall gains. A refiner and marketer absorbs the gap when pump prices are frozen, a city gas distributor faces higher input costs it cannot pass on immediately, and an airline pays more for fuel.

children.text: Domestic natural gas adds another layer of administered pricing. Gas produced from India's older fields is sold at a price set by a government formula linked to crude, with a floor and a ceiling, rather than at free market rates. Changes to that formula, and to how much cheap domestic gas is allocated to city gas distributors, can move the earnings of gas producers and distributors sharply, without any change in volumes. For city gas companies, the numbers to track are volumes in millions of standard cubic metres a day and the margin earned per unit sold.
Power: Where Regulation Guarantees the Return

India's power sector has three layers: generation, transmission, and distribution. Most large listed generators and the national transmission company operate under a regulated return model set by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission. The regulator allows a fixed return on the equity invested in an approved project, in the region of 15% or so, provided the plant meets availability norms. Fuel costs are largely passed through to buyers, and the generator earns a capacity charge for being available to supply, plus an energy charge covering fuel.

columns.label: Regulated, long-term contracted
points: Return on equity fixed by the regulator, subject to meeting availability norms
Fuel cost largely passed through to the buyer
Earnings grow mainly by adding new approved capacity, which grows the regulated equity base
Low risk, predictable, usually high dividend, valued on price to book

columns.label: Merchant power
points: Electricity sold on exchanges or short-term contracts at market prices
Fuel cost risk sits with the generator
Earnings swing with demand, weather, and coal availability
High risk, cyclical, closer to a commodity business

body.title: The Arithmetic of a Regulated Utility
body.prompt: A regulated power utility has ₹40,000 crore of regulated equity in approved projects, and the regulator allows a return on equity of 15.5%. Assuming it meets availability norms, roughly what profit does this regulated business earn, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹40,000 crore × 15.5% = ₹6,200 crore. Notice what this means for analysis. Growth does not come from selling more electricity at better prices; it comes from commissioning new approved capacity, which adds to the regulated equity base. So for these companies, track capitalisation of new projects and capex plans, not power demand alone.

body.title: The weak link: state distribution companies

children.text: Electricity in India mostly reaches homes and farms through state-owned distribution companies. Many sell power below cost because of subsidised tariffs for farmers and households, and lose more through technical and commercial losses. That leaves them short of cash, so they delay payments to generators and transmission companies. For an investor, this shows up as high receivable days on a generator's balance sheet: profits are reported, but the cash arrives late.

Successive government schemes have tried to fix this through debt restructuring, liquidity packages, late payment surcharge rules, and reform-linked funding. Progress has been real but uneven. When you analyse a power company, always check receivable days and how much of its dues are from state distribution companies, alongside the regulated return it reports.

stats.label: Regulated generator
stats.context: Track regulated equity, capacity added, plant availability, receivable days

body.title: The High Dividend Yield That Looks Too Good
body.scenario: A government-owned energy company trades at a P/E of 6 and offers a dividend yield of 8%. Its profits doubled last year. Your colleague says it is the cheapest large cap in India. You notice that the government holds a majority stake, last year's profits benefited from unusually wide margins, a new levy on the industry was introduced and later withdrawn, and the company is planning a large multi-year capital expenditure programme.
body.prompt: How would you evaluate this opportunity?
body.modelAnswer: Start by asking whether last year's profit is normal. Doubling profits in an energy business usually means unusually wide margins, whether refining spreads, marketing margins, or realisations on crude and gas. Apply the Chapter 2 lesson: calculate normalised earnings across a full cycle rather than using the peak year, and the P/E of 6 will look less extreme. The dividend yield is calculated on peak profits too, so ask whether the payout is sustainable once margins normalise and the capex programme starts consuming cash. Then assess policy risk in both directions: prices may be administered, levies can be introduced or withdrawn with little notice, and a majority government shareholder may have objectives beyond maximising profit, such as keeping fuel prices stable or funding strategic investment. Finally, look at the capex plan itself: does it earn a regulated or contracted return, or is it a merchant bet? A low multiple in this sector is often a permanent feature reflecting policy risk, not a temporary mispricing. That does not make it a bad investment, but the thesis has to be about normalised earnings and sustainable dividends, not about the headline P/E.

body.text: Valuation follows the risk model. Regulated utilities with predictable returns are usually valued on price to book and dividend yield, similar to how you valued banks in Chapter 3. Refiners and upstream producers are cyclical and are better judged on normalised EV/EBITDA. City gas distributors sit in between, with steady volumes but policy-driven input costs.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: The spread between the value of the products a refinery makes and the cost of the crude it processes is called the gross ___ margin.
body.explanation: GRM, quoted in dollars per barrel, is the core profitability measure for a refiner, and it matters more than the absolute level of crude prices.

body.title: Analysing an Energy or Utility Company
steps: Identify exactly which part of the chain the company operates in: upstream, refining, marketing, transmission, distribution, or generation
Establish who sets its prices: the market, a regulator, or the government
For refiners, track GRM per barrel, throughput, and the crude mix, and compare with benchmark margins
For marketers, separate marketing margin from refining margin and watch for pricing interventions
For regulated utilities, track regulated equity, new capacity commissioned, plant availability, and capex plans
Check receivable days and exposure to state distribution companies for power companies
Normalise earnings before applying any multiple, and treat high dividend yields on peak profits with caution

points: In oil, gas, and power, prices are often set by regulators or government policy rather than the market, which changes how each business behaves
The oil chain splits into upstream, refining, marketing, transmission, and distribution, and a crude spike affects each differently
Gross refining margin per barrel, multiplied by throughput, drives refiner profits; the absolute crude price matters less
Fuel marketers absorb the gap when pump prices are held steady, which can produce losses in a strong year for oil
Regulated generators and transmission companies earn a return on approved equity, so growth comes from commissioning new capacity
State distribution companies are the sector's weak link, so check receivable days alongside reported profits
Low P/E ratios and high dividend yields in this sector often reflect policy risk and peak earnings, so normalise before concluding a stock is cheap

body.text: Regulatory frameworks, administered gas pricing formulas, levies, and allowed returns change from time to time; the descriptions here are general and approximate. Figures in the worked examples are illustrative. Refer to CERC, PNGRB, the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, and company disclosures for current rules. Company names are examples, not recommendations to buy or sell any security.
